prompt: Ana applied `dev.tfvars` and then, in the same directory and the same state, asked for a plan with `prod.tfvars`. What did the plan propose?
hint: The state held one VPC when the plan started.

choices.text: A second network for prod, created beside the dev one
choices.why: That is what she expected. The state already held dev's VPC, so Terraform compared prod's values with it.

choices.text: Replacing dev's network
choices.why: Yes. One state, one VPC: the new range forces its replacement, and the subnet and security group inside it go too.

choices.text: Nothing, because a `.tfvars` file cannot change a resource that already exists
choices.why: Values feed the configuration like any other change; the plan proposed three replacements.

choices.text: An error saying the environment had changed
choices.why: Terraform has no idea what an environment is; it saw different values for the same resources.

prompt: In that same plan, with `prod.tfvars` against dev's state, how many resources would have been destroyed?
hint: Read the summary line of the plan.

prompt: As far as Terraform is concerned, what makes dev and prod two environments rather than one?
hint: What did the failed attempt have only one of?

choices.text: A separate `.tfvars` file for each
choices.why: Ana had two of those, and the second still rewrote the first environment.

choices.text: An `Environment` tag on every resource
choices.why: A tag is a value like any other; the plan just proposed changing it from dev to prod.

choices.text: A state of its own for each
choices.why: Right. A plan reads one state, and only a second state lets it see a second environment.

choices.text: Different names for the variables in each environment
choices.why: The variables are the same on purpose: same code, different values.

prompt: Which of these does giving each environment its own state provide? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of the options needs a layer below the state.

choices.text: A plan for prod that lists only prod's changes
choices.why: Yes; it reads prod's state and nothing else.

choices.text: Credentials for dev that cannot reach prod
choices.why: Two states in one account, read with the same keys, are separated by bookkeeping alone; that needs separate credentials or accounts.

choices.text: A lock per environment, so dev never blocks prod
choices.why: Yes; each state has its own lock.

choices.text: A dev mistake, applied, that damages dev alone
choices.why: Yes; prod's resources are not in dev's state for a plan to change.

choices.text: Smaller bills, since dev is built from cheaper values
choices.why: Cheaper values are a choice of values, not of state.

prompt: What does a workspace created with `terraform workspace new dev` start with?
hint: Read the message `new` printed.

choices.text: A copy of the `default` workspace's state
choices.why: It starts with nothing, which is why prod's first plan created everything.

choices.text: An empty state
choices.why: Yes. The configuration is the same; the state behind it is new.

choices.text: A new directory holding a copy of the configuration
choices.why: The directory and its files stay as they are; only the state changes.

choices.text: A bucket of its own for the state
choices.why: Same bucket, same backend block; the S3 backend files it under another key.

prompt: To name every resource after the state that owns it, Ana wrote `name = "shop-${___}"` in `main.tf`.
hint: The expression that holds the selected workspace's name.

prompt: Where does Terraform record which workspace is selected?
hint: Ana printed it with `cat`.

choices.text: In the state bucket, beside the states
choices.why: The bucket holds one state per workspace and no record of which one you chose.

choices.text: In `backend.tf`, which `select` rewrites
choices.why: `select` touches no file Ana wrote; `git diff` would show it if it did.

choices.text: In the shell's environment variables
choices.why: `TF_WORKSPACE` can override it for one command, but the selection itself is stored elsewhere.

choices.text: In `.terraform/environment`
choices.why: Yes: one word in a file `init` created, which git ignores.

prompt: After both workspaces were applied, why was `shop/terraform.tfstate` still in the bucket, without an `env:/` prefix?
hint: Which workspace keeps the plain key?

choices.text: It is the `default` workspace's state, emptied by the earlier destroy
choices.why: Right: 181 bytes of a state that holds nothing.

choices.text: It is a backup the S3 backend keeps of prod
choices.why: Backups of earlier writes are versions of the same key, not another key.

choices.text: It is the lock
choices.why: A lock is a `.tflock` object, and it disappears when the run ends.

choices.text: It is dev's state, because dev was created first
choices.why: Dev's state is under `env:/dev/`, like every workspace but `default`.

prompt: A colleague clones Ana's repository, runs `terraform init`, and plans with `prod.tfvars` without selecting anything. Which state does that plan read?
hint: Is the selection in anything the clone copied?

choices.text: Prod's, because that is what Ana selected
choices.why: Her selection is a file in her own `.terraform`, which git ignores; the clone never had it.

choices.text: Dev's, because it was the first workspace created
choices.why: Creation order decides nothing; a fresh checkout starts in `default`.

choices.text: `default`'s
choices.why: Yes, and with the destroyed state there it would plan to create a whole prod network beside the real one.

choices.text: None: Terraform refuses to plan until a workspace is selected
choices.why: There is always a selected workspace, and without a choice it is `default`.

prompt: Ana wants the `prod` workspace gone, with its resources removed rather than forgotten. Put the commands in order.
hint: Terraform refuses to delete a workspace that still tracks resources, or the one you are in.
trap: Deleting first is refused while the state tracks anything, and `-force` would leave the resources running with no record.

prompt: When Ana ran the plan with `dev.tfvars` while `prod` was selected, what on her screen said prod before the plan came back?
hint: Look at the line she typed.

choices.text: The prompt, which names the workspace
choices.why: It read `ana@laptop:~/shop$`, the same in every workspace.

choices.text: The name of the directory
choices.why: Workspaces keep one directory for every environment.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right, and that is the whole risk: the selection is a hidden file nobody reads.

choices.text: A warning from Terraform that prod was selected
choices.why: Terraform prints no such warning; it has no idea which workspace matters.

prompt: The `validation` block compares `var.environment` with `terraform.workspace`. Which mistake does it NOT catch?
hint: What does the comparison need to have in hand?

choices.text: `dev.tfvars` passed while `prod` is selected
choices.why: That is the accident it was written for, and it refused it.

choices.text: `prod.tfvars` passed while `dev` is selected
choices.why: Same comparison the other way round; it refuses this too.

choices.text: An edit to `main.tf` tried with prod selected
choices.why: Right. With prod's own values the two sides agree, and the untested change goes to prod.

choices.text: A values file whose `environment` line says `staging` while `dev` is selected
choices.why: `staging` is not `dev`, so the validation fails it like any other mismatch.

prompt: With `prod` selected, Ana ran `TF_WORKSPACE=dev terraform plan -var-file=dev.tfvars` and then `terraform workspace show`. What did `show` print?
hint: Does an environment variable write anything to disk?

choices.text: `dev`, since the variable selected it
choices.why: It selected dev for that one command and wrote nothing down.

choices.text: `prod`
choices.why: Yes. The stored selection is untouched, which is what makes the variable safe in a script.

choices.text: `default`, because the variable resets it
choices.why: Nothing resets it; the file still says prod.

choices.text: An error, because the variable and the file disagree
choices.why: They are allowed to disagree; the variable simply wins while it is set.

prompt: A pipeline holding only dev's credentials runs `terraform apply -auto-approve -var-file=prod.tfvars` with `prod` selected, by mistake. Prod lives in its own AWS account. What happens?
hint: Values and workspace agree here. What is left to stop it?

choices.text: The validation block refuses it
choices.why: `environment` is prod and the workspace is prod: the check passes.

choices.text: Terraform asks for a confirmation anyway, because the workspace is called prod
choices.why: Workspace names mean nothing to Terraform, and `-auto-approve` skips the question.

choices.text: It applies to prod, since every check agrees
choices.why: Every check in the configuration agrees, but the credentials cannot reach prod's account.

choices.text: It fails for lack of access, and prod is untouched
choices.why: Right. This is the layer below the state, and the one defence that does not depend on anybody choosing correctly.

prompt: In the directory-per-environment layout, how does Ana choose which environment a plan is for?
hint: Look at the prompt in the apply capture.

choices.text: With `-var-file`
choices.why: There is no values file to pass: the values are written into each directory's module calls.

choices.text: By running `terraform workspace select` first
choices.why: Each directory uses its `default` workspace; the directory itself is the choice.

choices.text: By the directory she runs it in, `envs/dev` or `envs/prod`
choices.why: Yes, and the prompt shows it on every line.

choices.text: With `TF_WORKSPACE`
choices.why: That variable picks a workspace inside one directory; here there is nothing to pick.

prompt: Why does each environment's `backend.tf` spell out its key, instead of taking it from a variable shared by both?
hint: Lesson 7 said when the backend block is read.

choices.text: S3 refuses object keys computed by Terraform
choices.why: S3 never sees how the string was produced.

choices.text: A backend block cannot use variables
choices.why: Right: it is configured before anything else is evaluated, so it is literal, or passed with `-backend-config`.

choices.text: So that `diff -r` shows the difference between the environments
choices.why: The diff shows it, but that is a consequence, not the reason.

choices.text: Terraform requires keys to be unique across all repositories
choices.why: Terraform knows nothing about other repositories; uniqueness is your job.

prompt: Ana added an `Owner` tag to the shared network module and planned in `envs/prod`. How many resources did prod's plan want to change?
hint: Prod has one VPC and one subnet per zone.

prompt: Ana wants dev to run a new version of the network module for a week while prod stays on the old one. Both directories use `source = "../../modules/network"`. What does she need?
hint: Where does a module source say which version it means?

choices.text: Nothing: prod only changes when somebody applies there
choices.why: Prod's next apply, for any reason at all, picks up whatever the path holds that day.

choices.text: A workspace called `trial` inside `envs/dev`
choices.why: A workspace gives another state, not another version of the code.

choices.text: Each environment to take the module by version, such as a git `?ref=`, instead of by path
choices.why: Right. Then dev moves to the new tag and prod stays where it is until somebody moves it.

choices.text: A copy of the new code in `envs/dev/backend.tf`
choices.why: The backend block says where the state lives, not what the module does.

prompt: What does Terragrunt do with the `remote_state` block in `root.hcl`?
hint: Look at the file found inside `.terragrunt-cache`.

choices.text: It keeps every unit's state on a Terragrunt server
choices.why: There is no such server; the states are in Ana's S3 bucket.

choices.text: It writes a `backend.tf` into each unit, keyed by the unit's path
choices.why: Yes: `live/dev/network/terraform.tfstate` for `dev/network`, one block written once.

choices.text: It replaces the S3 backend with one of its own
choices.why: The generated file is an ordinary S3 backend block that Terraform reads.

choices.text: It merges all the units into one state
choices.why: The opposite: every unit gets its own key, four of them here.

prompt: Why did the first `terragrunt run --all plan` in `live/dev` fail for the web unit?
hint: What does web need from network, and where does it come from?

choices.text: The network unit had no outputs yet, because nothing had been applied
choices.why: Right. A plan cannot read an output from a state that does not exist; mock outputs or an apply in order get past it.

choices.text: Terragrunt ran the two units in random order
choices.why: It printed the order first, network then web.

choices.text: The `dependency` block is spelt `dependencies`
choices.why: `dependency` is right; the error is about its outputs, not its name.

choices.text: moto cannot answer Terragrunt
choices.why: The network unit planned fine against moto, and the later apply worked.

prompt: Match each piece of the Terragrunt files with what it does.
hint: Two of them write files; one of them decides the order.

pairs.right: reads another unit's outputs and runs that unit first
generates `backend.tf` with a key from the unit's path
writes the provider block into each unit
gives the module's variables their values

right_distractors: runs one Terraform command in every unit below

prompt: Why does `root.hcl` set `terraform_binary = "terraform"`?
hint: Its own help names the default.

choices.text: To pin Terraform to the version in the lock file
choices.why: It names a program, not a version.

choices.text: Because the S3 backend only works with Terraform
choices.why: OpenTofu has an S3 backend too; the setting is about which program runs.

choices.text: Without it Terragrunt runs `tofu`
choices.why: Yes: `--tf-path` says the default is tofu on the PATH.

choices.text: So that Terragrunt can find modules in the registry
choices.why: Module sources have nothing to do with which binary runs.

prompt: In `live/prod`, somebody runs `terragrunt run --all --non-interactive apply`. How many times is a person asked to confirm before the units are applied?
hint: Two mechanisms skip a question each.

choices.text: Once per unit, as each Terraform apply asks
choices.why: Under `run --all`, Terragrunt adds `-auto-approve` to each one, so they do not ask.

choices.text: Once, for the whole queue
choices.why: That is Terragrunt's own question, and `--non-interactive` answers it.

choices.text: Not at all
choices.why: Right: `--non-interactive` answers Terragrunt's question and `-auto-approve` skips Terraform's.

choices.text: Twice: once for network, once for web
choices.why: Neither unit's Terraform asks under `run --all`.

prompt: A team wants a short-lived copy of the stack for every pull request, identical to the others, in one account, destroyed on merge. Which layout fits best?
hint: Creating one should be a single command.

choices.text: A directory per pull request
choices.why: Every pull request would add copied root files to the repository and remove them again.

choices.text: Terragrunt, with a unit tree per pull request
choices.why: It works, but it is the most machinery for copies that are identical and throwaway.

choices.text: Workspaces
choices.why: Yes: `workspace new`, apply, destroy, `workspace delete`, and nothing precious in any of them.

choices.text: One state shared by all the pull requests
choices.why: That is the first section's mistake: each would rewrite the others.

prompt: Dev and prod, one state each; prod in its own AWS account and kept one module version behind dev. Which layout fits best?
hint: Two environments, one state each: how much repetition is there to remove?

choices.text: Workspaces with a validation block
choices.why: One configuration cannot hold two module versions, and one backend block makes separate credentials awkward.

choices.text: A directory per environment
choices.why: Right: each directory has its own credentials and its own `?ref=`, and two copies are cheap.

choices.text: Terragrunt, because only it can pin modules per environment
choices.why: Plain directories pin per environment too; Terragrunt pays off when copies multiply.

choices.text: One directory and two `.tfvars` files
choices.why: One state for both, which is the replacement plan from the first section.

prompt: Which of these are true of all three layouts in this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Check each against workspaces, the odd one out.

choices.text: Each environment has its own state
choices.why: Yes; that was the problem all three solve.

choices.text: The environment shows in the path
choices.why: Not with workspaces: one directory for all of them.

choices.text: The modules' code can be shared between environments
choices.why: Yes; even workspaces share the whole configuration.

choices.text: Dev's credentials cannot reach prod
choices.why: That takes separate credentials or accounts, which no layout provides by itself.

choices.text: Terraform is the only tool to install
choices.why: Terragrunt is a second one.

prompt: Ana moves prod from workspaces to `envs/prod`, whose backend key is `envs/prod/terraform.tfstate`. The running prod network's state is still at `env:/prod/shop/terraform.tfstate`. What does `terraform apply` in `envs/prod` do?
hint: Which state does that directory read, and what is in it?

choices.text: It finds the old state through the `env:` prefix and plans no changes
choices.why: The prefix belongs to workspaces of the old configuration; this backend reads its own key and nothing else.

choices.text: It creates a second prod network beside the first
choices.why: Right: an empty state means create everything, lesson 7's duplicate again. Move the state first, as lesson 8 does.

choices.text: It refuses, because the VPC's range is already in use
choices.why: AWS accepts two VPCs with the same range; lesson 1 created exactly that.

choices.text: It adopts the running VPC because the tags match
choices.why: Terraform never matches resources by tag; only the state pairs an address with an id.

prompt: From nothing, somebody runs `terragrunt run --all apply` in `live/prod` and answers `y`. Put what happens in order.
hint: The dependency decides the middle.
items: Terragrunt lists the queue, network then web, and asks once
Terraform applies the network unit, with `-auto-approve`
Terragrunt reads the network state's output `vpc_id`
Terraform applies the web unit with that id as an input
trap: Web cannot go before network: its input is an output of a state that does not exist yet.

prompt: A colleague runs `terraform workspace delete -force prod` while prod still holds the running network. What is the situation afterwards?
hint: `-force` disables the check that refused Ana. What did the refusal warn about?

choices.text: The network is destroyed along with the workspace
choices.why: Deleting a workspace deletes the state, never the resources; that is why the check exists.

choices.text: The network keeps running and no state records it
choices.why: Right. Terraform has lost track of it, as the refusal said, and only an import can bring it back under management.

choices.text: The `default` workspace takes over prod's resources
choices.why: Each workspace has its own state; nothing is moved into `default`.

choices.text: Nothing changes until prod is selected again
choices.why: The state is gone at once; selecting `prod` again would start an empty workspace.
